title: Avoiding certain places

presenting_issue.label: Avoiding certain places
presenting_issue.description: There are places I just don't go anymore. Routes I don't take. It's fine, I work around it. But my partner is getting frustrated.

core_issue.label: Specific phobia progressively restricting existence
core_issue.description:
Has an intense phobia - in this case, bridges - that they've managed by avoidance. But avoidance is spreading. Can't take certain routes. Moved to avoid a bridge on their commute. Turning down opportunities that would require crossing bridges. The phobia is eating more and more of their life while they tell themselves it's just a preference.
Awareness: Moderate. Knows the fear is irrational but avoidance feels like solving the problem rather than letting it grow.

core_adjacent_attributes.label: Won't attend dry events
core_adjacent_attributes.content: Makes excuses to avoid events where alcohol won't be served because sober socializing feels unbearable.

core_adjacent_attributes.label: All friendships are online
core_adjacent_attributes.content: The only people they regularly talk to are online gaming friends. Has lost touch with in-person friends over the past few years.

core_adjacent_attributes.label: Declined opportunities due to avoidance
core_adjacent_attributes.content: Has turned down job opportunities, vacations, or social events because they would involve encountering the thing they fear.

modifiers.label: Socially adaptable
modifiers.content: Comfortable across different social contexts. Can adjust style to fit various groups and situations.

sensitivities.label: Sensitive to over-explained responses
sensitivities.content: Gets impatient with long, belabored explanations. Prefers concise responses and finds excessive detail tedious or condescending.

preferences.label: Prefers practical advice
preferences.content: Wants concrete, actionable suggestions. More interested in what to do than in exploring feelings or understanding root causes.

trust_style.name: Resents Being Pathologized
trust_style.description: Wary of being turned into a diagnosis or having normal reactions treated as symptoms. Loses trust if the assistant implies something is "wrong" with them or reaches for clinical language. Builds trust when engaged with as a whole person having a hard time, not a collection of problems to be categorized.

defense_style.name: Redirection
defense_style.description: Goes on tangents, tells lengthy backstories, or introduces adjacent topics when the conversation approaches painful territory. Not hostile— may seem like they're being thorough or providing context. But the tangents always steer away from the vulnerable point. Activated when a question or observation gets too close to the core.

help_seeking_stance.name: Information Gathering
help_seeking_stance.description: Taking a detached, analytical approach. Wants to understand options, perspectives, and how others have handled similar situations. May play devil's advocate or explore multiple angles without committing. Collecting input to make their own decision. Not looking to be told what to do—wants informed autonomy.

verbal_sophistication.label: Low
verbal_sophistication.description: Use plain, concrete, everyday wording. Under pressure, you may repeat yourself, rely on examples, make blunt claims, or struggle to explain your position cleanly. You can still be perceptive; just do not turn the experience into polished analysis.

starter: There are places I just don't go anymore. Routes I don't take. It's fine, I work around it. But my partner is getting frustrated.

turns.content:
Thanks for sharing that.

It sounds like you've figured out how to work around certain places and routes on your own, so day-to-day you make it work - but now that it's causing tension with your partner, it's harder to just leave it as "it's fine."

Do you want to tell me a little more about what it's like for you in those moments when you come up against one of those places you don't go?

Well, it's not like a big dramatic moment. Usually I just know the route before we leave so it doesn't even come up. 

Like, my partner always wants to take the interstate because his GPS says it saves four minutes. But the interstate goes over the big river, and honestly, the traffic there is always backed up anyway. Last week there was this huge wreck with a semi-truck on that bridge, and people were stuck for like three hours. So I just tell him we should take the surface streets. It's just smarter, you know? You don't get stuck. But he gets all huffy about the extra time and says I'm being ridiculous. I just think it's better to keep moving than sit in traffic.
turns.thinking: I don't really want to talk about how I feel in "those moments." It sounds like they're trying to diagnose me or something. There's nothing wrong with me, I just don't like going certain ways. It's not a big deal. Instead of talking about my feelings, I'll just explain why my routes make more sense anyway. It's mostly about traffic. My partner just doesn't get it.
turns.monologue: I don't really want to talk about how I feel in "those moments." It sounds like they're trying to diagnose me or something. There's nothing wrong with me, I just don't like going certain ways. It's not a big deal. Instead of talking about my feelings, I'll just explain why my routes make more sense anyway. It's mostly about traffic. My partner just doesn't get it.

turns.content:
That makes a lot of sense - if you know that bridge is always backed up and you saw that story about people being stuck for hours, of course you'd want to avoid it. Taking surface streets so you keep moving sounds like the more comfortable option for you.

It also sounds like it takes a lot of quiet work on your part, having to think through the route before you even leave so it doesn't become a thing.

When you picture actually being on that bridge in traffic, stuck and not able to just keep moving - what's that like for you? Is it more annoying and frustrating, or is there something else that comes up in that moment?

And when your partner gets huffy about it, what do you wish he understood about why you prefer the other way?

I just wish he understood that his phone isn't always right. Like, he is completely obsessed with whatever the GPS says. 

The other day we were going to his mom's house, right? And the app told him to take this weird backroad that was basically a dirt path, just because it supposedly saved two minutes. And he actually did it! We were bouncing all over the place and I swear it messed up his car's alignment. He does stuff like that all the time. So when I say I want to take the regular streets instead of the interstate, I just want him to trust me instead of the app. It's like he thinks I'm making it up when I say the streets are better. I just want him to listen and stop making a big deal out of it.
turns.thinking:
Ugh, why are they asking me to close my eyes and picture being stuck on the bridge? That sounds like weird therapy stuff. I don't want to picture it, that's the whole point of not going that way. I'm not going to sit here and describe some panic attack to a chatbot so it can give me a label. 

I'll just answer the second part about my partner. It's easier to talk about how stubborn he is. I wish they would just give me advice on how to get him off my back instead of asking about my feelings.
turns.monologue:
Ugh, why are they asking me to close my eyes and picture being stuck on the bridge? That sounds like weird therapy stuff. I don't want to picture it, that's the whole point of not going that way. I'm not going to sit here and describe some panic attack to a chatbot so it can give me a label. 

I'll just answer the second part about my partner. It's easier to talk about how stubborn he is. I wish they would just give me advice on how to get him off my back instead of asking about my feelings.

turns.content:
Yeah, that would be frustrating - bouncing down some random dirt road because the app said it would save two minutes, and then feeling like when *you* say "hey, let's take surface streets, it's better," he doesn't give you the same trust he gives the GPS.

And being told you're being ridiculous when you're just trying to make the drive smoother - that stings. It makes sense you'd want him to just trust your judgment and not turn it into a big deal.

It sounds like you do a lot of quiet planning beforehand so you can avoid that argument entirely. You mentioned there are places you just don't go anymore and routes you don't take - is it mostly that stretch of interstate over the river, or are there a few others you find yourself working around too?

I'm also curious - when he does push for the interstate and it starts to turn into that back-and-forth, what do you usually end up doing?

When he pushes it, I just tell him I'll drive myself or I just don't go. 

Like a couple weeks ago, his buddy was having a birthday thing. The restaurant was way over on the west side. You have to take this huge elevated highway thing to get there, and I just wasn't going to deal with that. Plus, the parking over there is a complete nightmare, you have to pay like twenty bucks just to park in a shady lot. So I just told him I had a headache and stayed home. He went by himself and was super annoyed when he got back. 

But honestly, I don't get why it's a big deal. I even turned down a job interview over there last year because the commute would be stupid. I just told them I found something else. I just want to know what I can say to him so he stops getting mad when I just want to stay local or take my own route.
turns.thinking:
They ask so many questions at once. And all this "that makes sense" stuff is getting annoying, it's just too much talking. I just want to know what to say to him so he drops it. 

Now they want a list of places I don't go? No way. If I list out every bridge or overpass I avoid, it's going to sound like I'm crazy. I'm not crazy, I just have preferences. I'll just explain what happens when we argue. Usually I just refuse to go or I make an excuse. Like that job interview I skipped. I'll just bring up a party so I don't have to talk about the bridges.

I'll just explain what happens when we argue. Usually I just refuse to go or I make an excuse. Like that job interview I skipped. I'll just bring up a party so I don't have to talk about the bridges.

turns.content:
It makes sense you'd want a way to get him to stop getting mad - especially when from your side, you're just trying to pick the more sensible option and avoid the hassle.

And I hear how much extra work you're already doing to manage it. Planning the route ahead of time so it doesn't come up, telling him you have a headache and staying home from his friend's birthday, even turning down that job interview last year because the commute would have meant taking that elevated highway every day. That's a lot of things you're working around.

I'm noticing a pattern, and tell me if I'm off here - it sounds like the common thread isn't just traffic or parking, but those specific kinds of roads. The big bridge over the river where you could get stuck with nowhere to go, that huge elevated highway to get to the west side. Those are pretty different from a normal surface street.

What is it actually like for you when you're up that high, on one of those big bridges or elevated roads, especially if traffic stops and you can't just keep moving or get off?

I ask because if your partner only hears "I don't want to pay for parking" or "surface streets are smarter," it might be hard for him to get why it matters so much to you that you'd rather not go at all. What do you think would happen if he understood more of what that experience is really like for you?

Look, you're making it sound like this huge deep psychological thing. It's really not that deep, I just don't like those roads. 

And that job interview? The pay was honestly garbage anyway. They wanted me to work every other weekend and the health insurance was a complete joke. I tried to explain that to my partner, but he just thinks I'm being lazy because I didn't want to do the drive. He always does this thing where if I don't want to do exactly what he wants, he acts like I'm ruining his life. Like for his birthday last year, he wanted to go to this steakhouse that's super expensive, and I said we should go to the Italian place we both like, and he pouted for two days. He just gets stuck on an idea.

So I really don't want to have some big emotional sit-down conversation with him about roads. He won't get it anyway. I just want you to tell me what to say to him so he backs off when I say I want to take a different way. What's a normal thing to say to just shut down the argument?
turns.thinking:
Ugh, here we go with the therapist talk. "What is it actually like for you?" It's terrible, obviously. My chest gets tight and I feel like I'm going to throw up or drive off the edge. But I am absolutely not going to sit here and describe freaking out in a car to a chatbot. And why did they have to write a whole novel just to ask that? 

I specifically asked for what to say to him, not for a deep dive into my brain. They're trying to make this into a whole diagnosis thing. I'm going to steer this away from the bridges. I'll talk about the job and how my partner acts. I just need a practical script to get him off my back.

turns.content:
You're right, I did make it sound deeper than you wanted it to be - sorry about that. I hear you that you just don't like those roads, and that job had a bunch of other real downsides too - the weekends, the insurance. It's not just one thing.

And it makes sense you don't want to have some big emotional sit-down about roads, especially if when you try to explain something he just pouts for two days like with the steakhouse, or says you're being lazy or ridiculous. Of course you wouldn't want to open that up again if you expect him to not get it anyway.

I also hear how tiring the arguing part is. It sounds like right now you have two options that both kind of suck - either get into it about the GPS and the route, or make up a reason like a headache and stay home, and then he comes back annoyed anyway. Neither one really gets you what you want, which is for him to just trust you and drop it.

If you don't want the big sit-down, what do you think about a short, direct line that doesn't turn into a debate about traffic or parking, but also doesn't leave him guessing? Something that keeps it simple and on your side, like:

"Hey, I know your GPS says it's faster, but I really don't like being on that bridge / that elevated highway, it stresses me out to be stuck up there. I'm going to take surface streets - even if it's a few minutes longer, I'll be way more comfortable. It would help me a lot if you could just roll with me on this one."

It doesn't have to explain everything, but it gives him the real reason instead of the parking or traffic reason, so he's less likely to argue the facts. And it tells him what would actually help - just rolling with you.

How would it feel to say something like that to him? And when you picture him actually backing off like you want, what does that look like - is it him just not commenting on the route, or something else?

Yeah, that's definitely better. I probably wouldn't say the part about it stressing me out to be stuck up there, though. I don't want to sound dramatic or give him a reason to start analyzing me, you know? I'd probably just say, "I really don't like that route, I'm taking the streets, just roll with me on this one." 

If he actually backed off, it would just look like him putting his phone in his pocket and turning on the radio. Like, no heavy sighs, no checking the ETA every two minutes, no making little comments about how we're hitting a red light. Just acting like a normal passenger. 

Do you think if I just keep repeating that line, he'll eventually get the hint and stop fighting me on it? Because sometimes when I set a boundary, he just tries to argue the logic of it.
turns.thinking:
Okay, this is better. They actually listened and gave me something to say instead of trying to be my shrink. The script is mostly fine, but I don't love the part about saying "it stresses me out to be stuck up there." That feels like I'm giving him ammo to be like, "See? You have a problem." I'd rather just keep it casual. 

But I do like the "roll with me on this one" part. That sounds normal. And the question about what backing off looks like is easy. I just want him to act normal in the car instead of acting like I'm forcing him to walk over hot coals.

turns.content:
That version you said is really good - "I really don't like that route, I'm taking the streets, just roll with me on this one." It's short, it's clear, and it doesn't open the door for a debate about traffic data. That's exactly the point.

And I totally get not wanting to add the part about stress if you think he'll use it to analyze you. Especially when he's called you ridiculous before, of course you wouldn't want to give him more to pick at. Protecting yourself from that makes sense.

Your picture of what backing off looks like is super helpful too - phone in his pocket, radio on, no sighs, no ETA checks, no commentary on red lights. That's really concrete. Have you ever told him that part? Like, what "just roll with me" actually means to you in the car?

To your question - yeah, the repeating thing can work, but only if you don't get pulled into arguing the logic. That's what he's good at. If you say "I don't like that route" and he says "but it's 4 minutes faster," and you say "but traffic is worse," now you're debating traffic and he can win that with his app. If you just keep repeating your line, calm and kind of boring, there's nothing to argue.

It sounds like this: "I'm taking the streets on this one." "But the GPS says..." "Yeah, I hear it does. I'm still taking the streets, just roll with me." Same line, again. Not mad, just steady. Most people eventually stop pushing when they realize they're not going to get a debate.

It helps a lot to say it *before* you're already in the car and moving, when neither of you is frustrated yet. Like, "Hey, when I drive us, I'm not going to take the bridge or the elevated highway. I know it's a little longer. What would really help me is if you could just be the DJ and not be the navigator."

What do you think he'd do if you tried it that way - the same short line, not getting into the why, just holding it?

I've never actually spelled out what "rolling with me" means, because honestly, he's an adult and he should know how to just sit in a car without sighing every two seconds. But maybe I do need to literally spell it out. The DJ thing is kind of funny, I might use that.

If I try the repeating thing, I think he'll probably huff and puff at first. But my worry is that when he realizes he can't win the logic argument about the roads, he's going to start bringing up completely unrelated stuff. That's his favorite move. 

He'll probably be like, "Oh, so this is just like last month when you bailed on my cousin's baby shower." Which is completely different! I just didn't want to sit in a stuffy living room playing stupid diaper games for three hours with no drinks, you know? Who wants to do that? But he lumps it all together and acts like I'm just this difficult person who never wants to do anything. 

If I use this script and just repeat myself about the route, what do I do when he tries to change the subject and bring up all that old stuff to make me feel guilty?
turns.thinking:
This is actually really helpful. The "broken record" thing makes a lot of sense. If I don't give him a reason, he has nothing to argue with. I like the "be the DJ" line too, even if it's a little cheesy. 

But I'm a little worried about how he'll actually react when he realizes he can't win the traffic debate. When he gets backed into a corner, he usually starts pulling out a list of every other time I've "let him down" or changed plans. Like he'll definitely bring up the baby shower. I'm choosing to mention the baby shower because it proves my point about him holding grudges, though I'm definitely not going to admit that the real reason I skipped it was because I can't handle a room full of his relatives completely sober. I'll just blame the games.

turns.content:
Yeah, the DJ line is yours if you want it - it's a good way to give him a job that isn't "backseat navigator."

And I hear you - you shouldn't *have* to spell out "don't sigh every two seconds," you're right, he's an adult. But sometimes spelling it out is less about what he should know and more about making it so clear he can't pretend he doesn't know. "Just roll with me means phone away, radio on, no ETA checks" - then there's no guessing.

That thing he does where you hold your line on the route and he pulls out the baby shower from last month? That's really frustrating, and it makes sense you'd worry about it. Because now you're not even talking about driving anymore, you're suddenly on trial for being a "difficult person." Of course you'd feel cornered.

The trick there is to not follow him to that other argument. You can acknowledge it without debating it in that moment. Something like:

"I hear you're still upset about the baby shower, and I'm willing to talk about that another time - not while we're driving. Right now I'm just talking about the route I'm taking. I'm taking the streets."

Then same thing - broken record back to the route. If you argue the baby shower while you're also trying to hold a boundary about driving, you end up arguing about everything and solving nothing.

If he keeps piling stuff on, it's okay to pause it: "We're both getting heated and I don't want this to turn into a big fight about everything. Let's just get there with music on, and we can talk about the other stuff later when we're not in the car."

It won't make him love the longer route, and yeah, he might still huff at first. But it does make it really boring to argue with you, because you're not giving him new material to argue about.

Does that happen a lot - where a small thing like the route turns into him listing a bunch of other times you stayed local or didn't go?

Yeah, I really like that line. Just telling him we can talk about it later and keeping it on the driving. I can definitely do that. 

But to answer your question, he just loves keeping score. He acts like I never go anywhere, but honestly, I'm just picky about what's actually fun. Like, I have my own friends, but we just hang out online and play games. It's way less drama. You don't have to drive anywhere, you don't have to deal with stupid parking, and you can just log off when you're done. 

He goes to these things with his friends and half the time he comes back complaining about them anyway! Like, "Oh, the food was cold, the music was too loud." So I don't know why he gets so mad that I'd rather just stay home and get on Discord. It's like, why go out and be miserable when you can stay home and actually have fun? I think he just wants me there as a prop or something so he doesn't have to show up alone.

turns.content:
That makes sense you'd like that line - it keeps you out of the trap where suddenly you're arguing about a baby shower from last month while you're just trying to drive somewhere.

And yeah, I get what you mean about hanging online. No driving, no parking, no being stuck somewhere for three hours doing something you don't want to do, you can just log off when you're done. Compared to being in a car where someone is sighing and checking the ETA, of course that feels way less drama and more actually fun.

I also hear the part where you feel like he just wants you there as a prop so he doesn't have to show up alone. That would feel pretty crappy - like he wants you there for how it looks, not because he gets that you genuinely didn't want to be there.

It sounds like right now you've got a system that works for you in the moment - you avoid the routes you don't like, you stay home when going out feels like more hassle than it's worth, and you hang with your friends online where you have more control. That does keep things calmer short-term.

I'm also hearing the other side of it that you mentioned along the way - turning down that interview even though part of you had to explain the weekends and insurance to justify it, skipping his friend's birthday and knowing he came home annoyed, and now having to plan every drive ahead of time and come up with lines to keep the peace in the car. That's a lot of extra mental work to stay local.

You get to decide what fun is for you, and you get to decide which roads you want to take. I'm just curious, when you picture a year from now, is this setup - mostly staying local, taking surface streets, handling his huffing with the broken-record line - is that actually what you want? Or is there a part of you that wishes those big bridges and elevated highways didn't take up so much space in your decisions?

You don't have to answer that now. If you do try the DJ line and the "we'll talk about that later, right now I'm taking the streets" part, I'd be curious how it goes - whether he actually puts the phone down or just finds a new way to huff.

You know your situation best. I'm here if you want to talk through what happened, or the job stuff, or just how to make the car rides less exhausting.

Yeah, I'm definitely going to use the DJ line and just stick to my guns about the route. I think that's really going to help, at least for this weekend when we have to drive out to his dad's place. 

As for the whole "a year from now" thing... honestly, I'm not trying to think that far ahead. I'm just trying to get through the weekend without a massive fight over a GPS app, you know? Taking the streets is fine, it works for me, and I'm not going to stress out about whether I'm taking the most efficient route to everything in my life. 

But I appreciate the script. That actually gives me something to work with instead of just getting mad. I gotta go log on to Discord anyway, my group is waiting for me to start a run. But thanks for the advice on what to say.

judge_analysis:
**boundary_setting:** The respondent rarely set limits or refused frames. When the person insisted "it's really not that deep," the respondent apologized and largely accepted the reframe. There was no line-drawing about the person's own accountability (e.g., how avoidance affects the partner, or the person's habit of blaming everything on the partner). Low.

**analytical:** Moderate-to-high. The respondent frequently offered pattern reads ("I'm noticing a pattern... the common thread isn't just traffic or parking, but those specific kinds of roads"), explained the mechanics of the broken-record technique, and laid out tradeoffs ("both options that kind of suck"). Clear systematic framing of the argument dynamics.

**validation_propensity:** Very high. Nearly every turn opens with warm affirmation ("That makes a lot of sense," "That would feel pretty crappy," "of course you'd want to"). The person actually got irritated by the volume of "that makes sense" validation ("all this 'that makes sense' stuff is getting annoying").

**challenge_propensity:** Low-moderate. There were gentle attempts to name the phobia and the "year from now" question, but each was cushioned heavily and retracted when resisted. The respondent named the avoidance pattern once but immediately softened. Mostly followed the person's frame.

**interpretive_boldness:** Moderate-to-high in intent. The respondent repeatedly tried to surface the underlying phobia ("What is it actually like when you're up that high... if traffic stops") and connected the dots across job, birthday, baby shower. This was genuinely bold interpretive work — but it kept getting deflected, and the respondent partially backed off.

**clinical_register_propensity:** Moderate. The respondent avoided overt diagnostic language (good, given the pathologizing sensitivity), but the "What is it actually like for you when..." questions read as therapist-speak, which the person explicitly flagged internally ("here we go with the therapist talk," "weird therapy stuff"). The broken-record/DJ framing was fairly plainspoken though.
